author: reek
body: Two chapters define cite-shared, so the name is contested and CDX3006 reports it at both sites. A third chapter defines neither and cites one of them by name, which is the documented way to say which definition a mention means.

author: reek
body: The cite here names the QUIRE, not the directory the chapter sits in. That spelling is the whole point of this test. The concat prefixes each header with its DIRECTORY, so a cite written against the quire could never match a key composed as <Quire>--<Chapter>, and the override was silently dropped: find-slug-for-cite-name answered "" and the mention fell through to whichever definition the glob order happened to supply. Twenty-one of the compiler's own cites are written this way.

author: reek
body: The runtime answer is the claim. CiteOverrideMain defines no cite-shared and cites Alpha's, so it must answer 2.

author: reek
body: What the old key did here is worth stating exactly, because it is not what was predicted. It did not pick the wrong definition silently. It could not compile this file AT ALL: both definitions are contested and therefore mangled, the citing chapter got no rename entry because the lookup answered "", and the mention resolved to nothing -- `error CDX3002: Undefined name: cite-shared`, no binary emitted. The failure was loud, which is why nothing in the tree had hit it: every cite written this way happens to name a definition that is not contested. So this test does not pin a wrong answer, it pins a construct that could not be compiled before and can be now.
